newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk coalition steels itself for censure vote.
newsitem.headline: Turk coalition steels itself for censure vote.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition massed its forces on Wednesday ahead of a parliamentary challenge by the secularist opposition that was expected to rattle but not topple the government.
Conservative leader Tansu Ciller met with her MPs behind closed doors in an effort to enforce party discipline in support of her coalition partner, Necmettin Erbakan of the Islam-based Welfare Party.

Senior Ciller aides said they were confident they could hold virtually all of their 121 deputies when the 550-seat body begins debate at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT) on an opposition bid to hold a censure vote on the government's foreign policy.
For its part Welfare, whose iron discipline effectively bars dissent, boasts 160 MPs. Together that gives the ruling coalition a margin of five seats beyond the 276 needed to guarantee victory.

Despite this cushion, the government can expect a rough ride from opposition MPs, frustrated by increasing gridlock and angered by Erbakan's bid to redirect foreign policy from the West and toward the Arab and Moslem world.
"It's clear the opposition's...attack will not be enough to topple Erbakan, but (he) will get hammered in the debate," political analyst Derya Sazak wrote in daily Milliyet.
"Today's parliamentary session will be worth watching. It is the opposition's day."

Erbakan's "eastern policy" blew up in his face 10 days ago when Libyan leader Muammer Gaddafi used an Erbakan visit as a platform to blast NATO-member Turkey's ties to the West and its treatment of its Kurdish minority.
Erbakan's stunned silence in the face of these remarks, as well as his own anti-Western rhetoric while in Libya, provoked condemnation at home and a broadside from the U.S. State Department.

Closer to home, inflation is running at 80 percent, and many bankers and other analysts expect it to burst into triple digits. Huge budget deficits have fed sky-high interest rates, robbing the economy of funds needed for investment.

The Turkish lira, meanwhile, sinks against the dollar each day. And foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have all warned of dire consequences if the government does not take matters in hand.
On Tuesday, a confident Erbakan assured his party faithful the government would emerge unsathed, and even strenghtened, from its first test since taking power on June 28.
"This vote will strengthen the government further. The government will be a lot stronger, it will continue on its way," the veteran Welfare leader said.
"We will serve until the year 2000," he vowed.
